extra.message: Hardcoded Default Secrets (Session Secret and Database Credentials) — If .env is not overridden in production, an attacker who knows the default SESSION_SECRET can forge session cookies and impersonate any user. The hardcoded database credentials allow unauthorized database access if the database is network-accessible. [verified: Both SESSION_SECRET (config.py:13) and DATABASE_URL (config.py:12) hardcode well-known defaults with no runtime validation preventing their use in production; the session secret default enables session forgery (critical), and the database URL default exposes known credentials.]

Password reset token leaked to console and logs — Account takeover via password reset — attacker who can read logs obtains the reset token and sets a new password for the victim. [verified: The `print(f"[mock-email] password reset token for {email}: {token}")` at line 141 in `reset_request` outputs plaintext reset tokens to stdout/logs with no `DEBUG`/`APP_ENV` guard, leaking account-takeover tokens to anyone with log access.]

Password Reset Token Written to Logs — Anyone with access to application logs can obtain plaintext password reset tokens and take over any user account for which a reset was requested. [verified: Same unconditionally-guarded `print` as finding [1] — the plaintext password-reset token at line 141 is written to stdout/logs with no production guard, enabling account takeover by anyone who can read console or log output.]

Payment status mass assignment allows bypassing payment workflow — Managers can mark payments as 'paid' without actual payment processing and change any payment status without transition constraints [verified: PaymentIn.status is writable with no exclude flag and no status-transition validation; create_payment(line 62) and update_payment(lines 92-93) directly apply attacker-supplied status via model_dump()/setattr with only role+scope guards, allowing managers to inject 'paid' at creation or change any payment status arbitrarily.]

Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag — Session cookies transmitted over HTTP can be intercepted via network sniffing, allowing session hijacking and account takeover. [verified: Same issue as finding [0]: `_set_session_cookie` hardcodes `secure=False` unconditionally; no runtime mechanism (env var, config flag, middleware) ever sets the Secure flag, so cookies transit over unencrypted HTTP.]

User enumeration via registration endpoint response — Attacker can enumerate valid user emails in the system, enabling targeted phishing, credential stuffing, or password spray attacks. [verified: The `/register` endpoint returns HTTP 409 when the email exists (line 53-55) versus HTTP 201 for new accounts; distinct status codes enable straightforward email enumeration.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Attackers can brute-force credentials across accounts without triggering lockout (by staying under 8 attempts per account), flood password-reset requests to generate excessive tokens, or perform credential stuffing at high velocity. [verified: Same as finding [3]: the codebase contains zero rate-limiting infrastructure — no library, middleware, or decorator — leaving login, registration, and password-reset endpoints open to high-velocity brute-force and token-generation attacks.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Brute-force attacks, password spraying across user accounts, registration spam, and resource exhaustion via unlimited password reset token generation. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware or decorator exists anywhere in the codebase (no slowapi, no custom limiter, no IP-based throttle); only per-account lockout after 8 failures which leaves password spraying and token-generation flooding unmitigated.]

User enumeration via account lockout response codes at login — Attackers can enumerate valid user accounts by observing HTTP 423 (locked) vs HTTP 401 (invalid/nonexistent) response codes at login [verified: The login endpoint returns HTTP 423 for locked accounts (line 84-85) before checking the password, while non-existent accounts return HTTP 401; the distinct status codes allow enumerating valid accounts by observing lockout responses.]

Missing rate limiting on password reset request endpoint — An attacker can flood the password reset endpoint to enumerate valid accounts, exhaust system resources, or harass users with excessive reset emails. [verified: No rate limiting mechanism exists anywhere in the codebase (no slowapi/limiter library, no middleware, no decorator); the reset_request endpoint is unauthenticated and reachable, allowing email flooding and resource exhaustion via repeated token generation and DB writes.]

CSV Formula Injection in Exports — An attacker who can inject formula characters into database fields (via ticket descriptions, tenant names, property names, etc.) can cause arbitrary command execution when an admin opens an exported CSV in a spreadsheet application. [verified: Same root cause as finding 0: `_csv_response` at line 182 emits all export data via `QUOTE_ALL` without formula-prefix escaping. Tenant `full_name`, `email`, `unit_number` and other user-controlled DB fields flow unsanitized into CSV cells — spreadsheet apps interpret leading `=`/`@`/`+`/`-` as formulas. No compensating control found in models, routes, or the writer call.]

CSV formula injection in data exports — Client-side code execution when exported CSVs are opened in spreadsheet applications — attacker-controlled formulas can execute commands, exfiltrate data, or install malware on the victim's machine. [verified: The `_csv_response` function (line 182) writes DB-sourced user data (ticket titles, tenant names, emails) into CSV cells using `csv.writer(buf, quoting=csv.QUOTE_ALL)` without sanitizing formula trigger characters (=, @, +, -). QUOTE_ALL wraps in quotes but does NOT prevent spreadsheet formula execution. No sanitization exists anywhere in the pipeline.]

CSV formula injection in maintenance ticket export — An attacker can inject spreadsheet formulas that execute when an admin opens the exported CSV, leading to code execution, data exfiltration, or credential theft in spreadsheet applications. [verified: Tenants can create tickets with formula-laced title/category (no role restriction on create_ticket, lines 105-108 of tickets.py); these fields flow unsanitized through MaintenanceTicket.title/.category → export_maintenance rows (line 241) → _csv_response (line 182 csv.QUOTE_ALL, which does NOT prevent formula execution). No sanitization of trigger characters (= + - @) exists anywhere in the pipeli]

Missing rate limiting on password reset completion endpoint — An attacker can brute-force password reset tokens to take over accounts, or exhaust system resources by flooding the reset completion endpoint. [verified: No rate limiting exists anywhere; the reset_complete endpoint is unauthenticated and reachable, though brute-forcing 256-bit secrets.token_urlsafe(32) tokens is infeasible, resource exhaustion via repeated DB lookups remains a valid low-severity concern.]

CSV formula injection in inspection export — An attacker can inject spreadsheet formulas that execute when a manager/admin opens the exported inspections CSV, leading to code execution or data exfiltration in spreadsheet applications. [verified: The export_inspections CSV includes unit.unit_number (line 269) which is user-controlled at unit creation. However, create_unit requires admin_or_manager (line 137 of properties.py), making this a same-privilege attack. The claim's mention of findings/notes is incorrect—those fields are NOT exported. Only unit_number is a viable vector, and csv.QUOTE_ALL provides no protection.]

CSV formula injection in payments export — An attacker can inject spreadsheet formulas via payment reference/method fields that execute when a manager/admin opens the exported payments CSV, leading to code execution or data exfiltration in spreadsheet applications. [verified: Payment.method flows from Payment model (user-controlled via create_payment requiring admin_or_manager at line 56 of payments.py) into export_payments CSV rows (line 294) with no formula sanitization. The claim incorrectly states 'reference' is exported—it is not. csv.QUOTE_ALL is ineffective against formula injection. Same-privilege attack (admin/manager both injects and exports).]

Lease status bypass on creation via unchecked status field — Managers can create leases in any status (e.g. 'active') bypassing the status transition workflow and incorrectly marking units as occupied [verified: LeaseIn.status field (schemas.py:107) accepts any LeaseStatus enum value from user input and payload.model_dump() at leases.py:76 passes it directly into Lease() with NO validation restricting creation to 'draft'. The _ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS check at line 105 is only in update_lease/transition_status, not in create_lease. Authenticated managers can bypass the draft→active workflow, but the impact is ]
